analysis.one_liner: Bans stock and crypto trading by members of Congress, top executive officials, Supreme Court justices, and Federal Reserve leaders.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it died when the 118th Congress ended, with no cosponsors and no action beyond its initial referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop members of Congress, the President and Vice President, Supreme Court justices, and top Federal Reserve officials — plus their spouses and young children — from owning or trading individual stocks, futures, commodities, or cryptocurrency, and would require them to sell any such holdings within 120 days. It would also force senior officials to report when they or their families apply for or receive federal money like contracts, grants, or loans, put a $1,000 fine on late trade-disclosure filings, and set a penalty of at least 10% of the value of any banned holding knowingly kept. It would move all financial disclosures and trade reports onto searchable public websites with downloadable data.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who currently have little practical way to see whether the officials writing laws and setting policy are trading on information those roles give them. Taxpayers benefit if officials can no longer personally hold stakes in companies affected by their decisions.

how_it_helps.text: Bans members of Congress, the President, Vice President, Supreme Court justices, Federal Reserve governors and bank presidents, and their spouses and dependent children from holding or trading individual securities, futures, commodities, and cryptocurrency, and requires divestiture within 120 days [S2].

Requires senior officials and their families to report, within 30 to 45 days, any application for or receipt of federal payments including contracts, grants, and loans, with a $5,000 fine for failing to report [S2].

Requires financial disclosure and transaction reports for members of Congress, senior executive branch officials, judicial officers, and Federal Reserve bank officers to be filed electronically and posted on public websites that allow searching, sorting, downloading, and API access [S2].
Sets a penalty of at least 10 percent of the value of any covered financial interest knowingly bought, sold, or held in violation of the ban [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, the President and Vice President, Supreme Court justices, and senior Federal Reserve officials, along with their spouses and children, who would have to sell individual stock holdings and hold only diversified funds, Treasury securities, or a spouse's work-related compensation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Senior federal officials and their families

drawbacks.text: Enforcement depends on officials self-reporting and on ethics offices policing their own oversight, and the bill replaces the existing criminal-fine language for late trade reports with a flat $1,000 fine, which is a modest penalty for late filings even as knowing violations draw a larger fine [S2].

Requiring divestiture of individual stocks could discourage some people with significant investment experience from serving in government, though the bill allows diversified mutual funds, Treasury bonds, and a spouse's employment compensation, which soften that effect [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — removing the possibility that officials who write laws and set policy also profit from individual companies affected by those decisions — addresses a conflict that is difficult for the public to detect under current disclosure rules. The costs are real but limited: forced divestiture may deter some wealthy candidates from serving, and self-reported enforcement is imperfect. On balance the design targets the conflict directly and leaves broad-market funds available, so the safeguards reasonably outweigh the compliance burden.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Gillibrand introduced it in December 2023, the Senate sent it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and no committee vote, floor vote, or cosponsor ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 18, 2023 and read twice [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, which took no further action on it [S4].
No senator joined as a cosponsor; the cosponsor list shows zero [S3].
The bill never received a committee markup or a vote in either chamber, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The officials the bill would have covered — members of Congress, Supreme Court justices, senior executive branch officials, and Federal Reserve leaders, along with their families — are better off, because they keep the ability to hold and trade individual stocks and other assets and to keep their current disclosure arrangements. Members of Congress in particular avoided being subject to a trading ban and divestiture requirement.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress and other covered officials

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York; sole sponsor of S. 3555
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and did not attract any cosponsors before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Gary Peters
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee vote or markup on the bill after it was referred to his committee; the bill stayed there for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: United States Senate
against.what_they_did: No senator from either party cosponsored the bill, and the Senate never debated or voted on it.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote to break down by party; the only visible signals are one Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and no committee or floor action.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and other covered senior officials (President, Vice President, Supreme Court justices, Federal Reserve leaders)
industries.note: The bill would have banned them and their spouses and young children from holding or trading individual stocks, futures, commodities, and cryptocurrency and required divestiture within 120 days, with fines of at least 10 percent of the value of violating holdings. Their personal financial interest in keeping those holdings ran directly against the public's interest in officials without tradable financial conflicts, and the bill died before they had to give anything up [S2].

industries.industry: Federal Reserve bank presidents, vice presidents, and directors
industries.note: The bill would have applied the STOCK Act's disclosure and trading rules to these officials for the first time and put their filings on a public, searchable database, ending an exemption that had kept their finances out of the standard disclosure system [S2].
